title: Scythia
capsule: The Scythians were Iranian-speaking horse-nomads who dominated the Pontic-Caspian steppe from roughly the 7th century BC, when they displaced the Cimmerians and penetrated as far south as the Near East, to the late 3rd century BC when the Sarmatians pushed them west and confined them to Crimea. Herodotus provides the most extensive ancient account of their territory and tribal divisions, placing the Royal Scythians on the lower Dnieper and Bug; Scythian burials (kurgans) with gold-rich grave assemblages from Ukraine to Kazakhstan attest a vast but loosely integrated cultural sphere. The Macedonian campaign of Philip II and his son Alexander tested Scythian power c. 339 BC when Philip defeated the Scythian king Ateas; by the 3rd century BC Sarmatian pressure had reduced Scythia proper to the Crimean peninsula, where a rump kingdom survived until the 3rd century AD.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Scythian territorial extent is archaeological and textual, derived from kurgan distribution and Herodotus' geographic account; the dataset geometry for Scythia necessarily reflects a broad cultural zone rather than a bounded polity, and eastern limits are highly conjectural.
